analysis.one_liner: Opens more federal offshore waters to oil and gas drilling, letting coastal governors nominate areas for leasing.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its House subcommittee and received no vote before the 113th Congress ended, leaving the existing offshore leasing plan in place.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have thrown out the government's existing five-year plan for offshore oil and gas leasing and ordered a new one covering 2016 through 2020. Under the new plan, the governor of any coastal state could nominate the federal waters off that state's coast for drilling, and those areas would automatically go into the draft plan. The Interior Secretary could only leave out a nominated area if drilling there could not be safely mitigated and would not serve the national economic interest, and would have to justify that decision in writing to the governor.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies, which would gain access to lease and drill in Atlantic, Pacific, and Eastern Gulf waters that the current plan keeps off-limits. Coastal state governors who want drilling off their shores would gain new power to put those waters into the leasing plan. The bill's sponsors argued that expanded drilling would create energy jobs and reduce reliance on foreign oil.

how_it_helps.text: The bill scraps the existing 2012-2017 leasing plan, which the bill text notes excludes the entire Atlantic Coast, the entire Pacific Coast, and nearly all of the Eastern Gulf of Mexico, and orders Interior to write a new five-year program in its place.
It lets a coastal state's governor nominate federal waters adjacent to that state for drilling and requires those nominated areas to be included in the draft leasing program.

The Secretary can exclude a nominated area only by determining that drilling impacts cannot be effectively mitigated and that development is not in the national economic interest, and must then report the reasons to the governor and the House Natural Resources Committee.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, coastal communities and the tourism, fishing, and seafood industries near newly opened waters would have borne the risk of spills and industrial activity off their coasts. The general public would have borne the environmental risk of drilling in largely unexplored waters, while the bill's own text acknowledges most of these areas have been little explored, meaning resource estimates would have to be developed with limited data.

drawbacks.text: Opening previously off-limits coasts to drilling exposes coastal economies built on tourism and fishing to the risk of spills and drilling activity, and the bill's own text concedes the newly covered areas are largely unexplored, so resource estimates would rest on thin data.

By requiring state-nominated areas to be included in the draft program unless the Secretary meets a two-part test and files a written justification, the bill shifts the default in federal leasing decisions toward drilling and gives a single state governor outsized influence over federal waters that belong to the whole country.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the oil and gas industry, the benefits are direct: more waters to lease and drill. For the public, the promised gains — jobs and energy supply — are uncertain, since the bill targets areas the current plan deliberately leaves out, while the costs fall on a narrow set of coastal places that bear the spill risk whether or not drilling pays off for them. On balance the bill's value flows mainly to one industry, and its death in committee meant those trade-offs were never tested in a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, then to its Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee, and nothing further happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Kevin Brady of Texas introduced the bill on June 5, 2013, with Reps. Wittman and Shimkus as original sponsors, and it was sent to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
Five days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, and no further action was ever recorded.
Thirteen House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote, and the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, leaving the existing 2012-2017 offshore leasing program in place.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coastal tourism, fishing, and seafood interests are better off because no new drilling areas were opened off the Atlantic, Pacific, or Eastern Gulf coasts. The oil and gas industry lost the chance to expand into those waters but faced no new restrictions either.

for.name: Rep. Kevin Brady
for.role: Sponsor, House Natural Resources Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing Interior to replace the existing offshore leasing plan with one friendlier to expanded drilling.

for.name: 13 of 435 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all recorded cosponsors were Republicans.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over offshore leasing
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittee on June 10, 2013 and never brought it to a committee vote or reported it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 cosponsors were House Republicans and there is no recorded Democratic support; the bill made no progress in a Republican-controlled committee either.

industries.note: The bill would have opened Atlantic, Pacific, and Eastern Gulf waters for leasing, a direct expansion of drilling opportunities the current plan keeps off-limits. Its death preserved the status quo, so the industry gained nothing here.
These industries depend on clean coasts and fisheries, which new offshore drilling would have put at risk of spills and industrial activity. The bill's failure kept those waters closed.
